I received the following question by email:

> I was wondering if mathematical relationships exist between monthly, quarterly, and annual growth rates (percentage changes).
> For time series data ...<br>
> 1) Is there a mathematical formula to know by how many months the Month-to-Month changes lead turns in this-month-to-the-same-month-one-year-ago changes (annual changes)?<br>
> 2) Is there a mathematical formula to know by how many quarters the Quarter-to-Quarter changes lead turns in this-quarter-to-the-same-quarter-one-year-ago changes (annual changes)?<br>
> Also, regarding simple moving averages/totals:<br>
> 3) Is there an exact or approximate formula to know by how many months a 3-month simple moving average (or moving total) leads a turn in a 12-month simple moving average (or moving total)?<br>
> As an example: Inflation is typically measured with Y/Y percentage changes in the CPI.
> So, it would be helpful to be able to identify when the 12-month rate of change will likely reach a top or bottom, using the 1-month or 3-months rates of change.

## Monthly growth vs year-over-year growth

Suppose we have monthly data $y_1,y_2,\dots$.
Then the monthly growth rates are given by $g_t = \frac{y_t - y_{t - 1}}{y_{t - 1}}$, and the year-over-year growth rates are given by $G_t = \frac{y_t - y_{t - 12}}{y_{t - 12}}$.
Some algebraic manipulation leads to
$$
  1 + G_t = \prod_{j = 1}^{12} (1 + g_{t - j + 1}).
$$
So the year-over-year rate is the compounded product of the last 12 monthly rates.
A useful recurrence relationship is
$$
  \frac{1 + G_t}{1 + G_{t - 1}} = \frac{1 + g_t}{1 + g_{t - 12}}.
$$
Therefore
$$
  G_t > G_{t - 1} \iff g_t > g_{t - 12}.
$$
In other words, the year-over-year rate rises when the current monthly change is larger than the change 12 months ago, and it falls when the current monthly change is smaller than the change 12 months ago.

For example, annual inflation peaks when the monthly inflation rates entering the 12-month window become smaller than the monthly inflation rates dropping out of the window.
Because year-over-year growth is effectively a 12-month trailing window of monthly growth, its average timing is centered about 5.5 months in the past.
In general, for smooth series, the month-to-month rate often leads the year-over-year rate by about **5 to 6 months**.

## Log growth rates

Taking logarithms turns the multiplicative relationship above into a linear one, which is often more convenient for compounding over several periods, forecasting, or working with series such as price indices where growth is conventionally expressed in log form.

Define monthly log growth $\ell_t = \ln(1 + g_t)$ and year-over-year log growth $L_t = \ln(1 + G_t)$, using $g_t$ and $G_t$ from above.
Taking logs of the product identity $1 + G_t = \prod_{j = 1}^{12}(1 + g_{t - j + 1})$ turns the product into a sum:
$$
  L_t = \sum_{j = 0}^{11} \ell_{t - j}.
$$
So $L_t$ rises when $\ell_t > \ell_{t - 12}$, the same turning condition as before, but now a linear relationship rather than a multiplicative one.

This also gives a forecasting formula:
$$
  L_{t + h} = L_t
              + \sum_{s = 1}^{h} \left(\ell_{t + s} - \ell_{t + s - 12}\right).
$$
So given assumptions about future monthly growth, you can forecast the future year-over-year rate exactly in log terms.

The same idea works over any horizon, comparing the most recent 3-month block to the corresponding block a year earlier:
$$
  L_t
  - L_{t - 3} = \sum_{j = 0}^{2} \ell_{t - j}
  - \sum_{j = 0}^{2} \ell_{t - 12 - j}.
$$
So the year-over-year rate has risen over the past three months if recent 3-month growth is higher than the corresponding 3-month block from one year ago.

This is exactly how CPI inflation is usually reported: with $y_t$ the price index, $\ell_t$ is monthly inflation and $L_t$ is the standard year-over-year inflation rate quoted in the news.

## Quarterly growth vs year-over-year growth

The quarterly version is exactly analogous: just replace 12 by 4.
Since four-quarter growth is a trailing 4-quarter window of quarterly growth, its average timing is centered about 1.5 quarters in the past.

## 3-month moving averages/totals vs 12-month moving averages/totals

A *trailing* [simple moving average](https://otexts.com/fpp3/moving-averages.html) of $\{y_1, y_2, \dots\}$ is defined as:
$$
  \hat{T}_{k,t} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j = 0}^{k - 1} y_{t - j}.
$$
Then
$$
  \hat{T}_{k,t} - \hat{T}_{k,t - 1} = \frac{1}{k} (y_{t} - y_{t - k}).
$$
So $\hat{T}_{k,t}$ rises when the newest observation entering the window, $y_{t}$, exceeds the oldest observation leaving the window, $y_{t - k}$, and falls when the reverse holds.

As with the growth-rate case, the practical lead between two moving averages of different lengths can be approximated from the center of each trailing window.
A trailing $k$-period average is centered about $(k - 1)/2$ periods in the past, so a 3-month average is centered about 1 month in the past, while a 12-month average is centered about 5.5 months in the past.
So for smooth cycles, a 3-month moving average tends to lead a 12-month moving average by about $5.5 - 1 = 4.5$ months, for exactly the same reason that monthly growth leads year-over-year growth above.
